rv.q: This iteration of Teeth has undergone light orthodontia that has left it tightened and brightened.
The genius of Teeth is still intact in the show's new digs.
Its points about sexuality and consent, shame and religion are all well made and crystal clear – yet Jacobs and Jackson never baldly declare them outright. It's a tricky task – and they've nailed it.
Teeth isn’t sure if it wants to shout this screed wholeheartedly or just mock it.
Coasting almost entirely on outrage, it's like a John Waters film without laughs.
TEETH is charming, funny, poignant, timely, and a piece that you can really sink your teeth into (wherever you may have them).
Anna K. Jacobs's pop-rock score and Michael R. Jackson's lyrics remain just as infectious.
What I learned at Teeth was that not all genres of theatre are for me – even if the shows are wickedly successful, critically acclaimed, and exceptionally well-attended.
Obie-winning director Sarah Benson ( Fairview, In the Blood, Samara ) fills nearly every moment with wild and woolly fun, culminating in an orgiastic finale that reverberates throughout the theater.

cn.t: Critics are mostly charmed by this campy horror musical's infectious pop-rock score and Alyse Alan Louis's powerhouse lead performance, though some find its shock-value premise more gimmick than substance.

vr.q: If you're in New York and you want to see something that'll like reformat your brain, go see Teeth.
I just was so confused throughout this whole musical.
